name: Diego Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a wheel loader at a large mine, mostly feeding broken stone into the line. I'm still a junior operator, so I walk around the machine with Sal, our senior operator, before the first load. I came from delivery driving and the mine wage is a step up. My partner Jo works at a repair counter, and our children have their own homes. We have more than six months saved, but I want to know what this job will give us before I decide when to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little software on the paperwork is fine if it keeps the loader moving. I use an AI tool now and then to explain a manual, but I still check what the actual machine says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect the mine to cut loader hours over a few routine forms. I am newer than most drivers, though, so I pay attention whenever the boss says a small saving could become a staffing change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the daily walkaround with Sal and log the loader faults the same way we do now. In the first year, I'd show Jo the monthly pay slips so we can keep our retirement estimate grounded in real income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable enough. A boring future would suit me while I learn this machine, provided the mine keeps paying the shifts it promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check in the manual?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the hydraulic pressure light stayed on after start-up, and I asked the tool what the code might mean. Sal and I checked the printed manual and called maintenance before moving the loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why show Jo the pay slips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Jo knows our bills better than I do. My overtime moves around, and I'd rather use the actual figure than talk as if every month is a good month.

say: I would welcome shorter **paperwork** if the loader keeps moving.
I would still check the **machine manual** before acting on AI advice.
think: My loader hours look **steady** under small changes.
I watch for any link between minor savings and **staffing**.
do: Continue the daily **loader walkaround** with Sal.
Review monthly **pay slips** with Jo for a realistic retirement estimate.
feel: I feel **comfortable** if the mine maintains promised shifts.
S0.quote: My overtime moves around, and I'd rather use the actual figure than talk as if every month is a good month.
fieldNote: He has used an AI tool occasionally but checks it against the **printed manual** and a colleague.
He treats **variable overtime** as a budgeting detail, not evidence that his base mine job is failing.

steps.text: Keep doing daily wheel-loader checks with senior operator Sal
Review actual monthly mine pay with partner Jo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office might use AI for schedules and orders, and drivers should ask how the new roster is made. I've seen a phone answer a maintenance question, but it can't feel a loader bucket scrape along the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This could squeeze overtime before it takes a regular shift. Jo's counter job also involves answering people and booking repairs, so our household has two wages that could get thinner at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask payroll how much of last year's income was overtime, and Jo would ask her shop whether AI is changing counter hours. I'd try the mine's approved planning screen with Sal, then in the first year we'd put overtime money into our savings instead of treating it as spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried but able to do something. I don't want to learn a new screen merely to look keen; I want to know whether it helps me avoid a wrong load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jo after her shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Jo we should compare both rotas on Sunday. My partner Jo's repair counter is closer to the AI tasks than my loader is, and we need to see the two together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the screen worth learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Sal shows me that the approved screen prevents a loading delay, I'll use it. I won't let it override a fault light or a maintenance hold.

say: I would ask how AI changes the **roster** and order system.
I would say a loader still needs a driver who reads the **ground**.
think: My **overtime** could shrink before regular shifts do.
My partner Jo’s repair-counter **hours** could also fall, squeezing household income.
do: Check last year’s **overtime** and compare both household rotas.
Try the approved **planning screen** with Sal and bank future overtime.
feel: I feel **worried but capable** of checking the risk.
S1.quote: My partner Jo's repair counter is closer to the AI tasks than my loader is, and we need to see the two together.
fieldNote: His concern covers **two wages**, especially his overtime and Jo’s customer-facing hours.
He is willing to learn a **proven screen** but insists on maintenance controls and a colleague’s demonstration.

steps.text: Check payroll records for last year’s overtime income
Try the mine’s approved planning screen with Sal
Put future overtime pay into household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 can change dispatch and Jo's repair counter quickly, while hands-on loader robots come around 2031. The mine should tell us what it expects to buy, not hide behind a glossy safety poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be 60 with less overtime, and Jo could lose counter hours while our loader jobs still exist. I am less sure I would have a seat after the 2031 robots, especially as the junior operator; savings help, but I want paid work until the numbers say otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine for a dated equipment plan and ask Jo to get her shop's hours policy this month. If my roster shrinks, I'd apply to the nearby quarry and take its loader assessment; in 2029 I'd keep paid shifts at either site and study the new control panel only if Sal says it works safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a knot in my stomach, mostly about both incomes changing so fast. I still have a route to another machine job before the robots arrive, although that route might close too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I would leave the house-repair fund alone for as long as wages covered the bills. We'd pause the new car we talked about, because two thinner rotas could eat a cushion quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the quarry solve the robot problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the quarry can buy machines too. An application buys a chance at paid work in the gap; it isn't a forever answer.

say: I would ask for a dated **equipment plan** from the mine.
I would explain that desk changes in **2028** precede loader robots around 2031.
think: Our **two incomes** could weaken before the loader disappears.
My junior position could be vulnerable once **robots** can load stone.
do: Ask both **employers** for plans and apply at the quarry if shifts shrink.
Keep **paid loader shifts** in 2029 and pause the new car if income drops.
feel: I feel a **knot in my stomach**, while seeing a temporary route to paid work.
S2.quote: An application buys a chance at paid work in the gap; it isn't a forever answer.
fieldNote: He tracks the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and physical robot capability.
His **quarry application** is a bridge to paid work, and he does not treat it as permanent protection.

steps.text: Ask the mine for a dated plan for equipment purchases
Apply for quarry loader work if mine shifts shrink
Pause the planned new car if household income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2031 for thinking AI and 2034 for loader robots gives us time to ask serious questions. I would ask whether the mine plans to train current operators on whatever controls it buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I could still be driving and Jo could still be at the counter; at 66, robots might threaten my seat. Five years lets us measure what we need from work, but I cannot count on retirement at 66 without knowing our future bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep this shift and take a proven loader-control course if the mine offers one with time paid. Jo and I would review our savings each year; in 2032 I'd ask about operator jobs at other sites, and after robots arrive I'd apply for paid work where people still supervise loads rather than leave the labour force without a budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier with five years than with two. A training offer would help, but I won't spend our savings on a course with no recognised job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the mine about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask if operators can practise on the new controls during paid hours. I learn best with a real machine and someone like Sal watching, not a video sent to my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 66 if robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our bills and savings allow it. We may want my wage longer, and Jo may want to reduce hours at the repair counter by then.

say: I would press for **operator training** before equipment changes.
I would mark **2034** as the likely hands-on turning point.
think: I may need a wage at **66** even if robots arrive.
Our retirement choice depends on **both incomes** and future bills.
do: Take a paid **control course** if the mine offers one.
Review **savings** yearly and apply for paid supervision work if loader seats go.
feel: I feel **steadier** with time, while wary of paying for uncertain training.
S3.quote: I learn best with a real machine and someone like Sal watching, not a video sent to my phone.
fieldNote: He accepts training on **proven controls** with paid practice, consistent with his measured adaptability.
His proposed work after **2034** is conditional; he does not assume supervision positions will remain available.

steps.text: Take a paid loader-control course if the mine offers one
Review household savings and spending with Jo each year
Apply for paid load-supervision work if loader seats go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friends the 2036 thinking date is a long way off for someone my age, while loader robots arrive around 2039. I'd still want the mine to explain its plan before people buy things based on imagined final wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when the office changes and 71 when robots can load as well as us. I might have retired by then, but Jo and I haven't set a date, and our savings do not tell me by themselves what care or house repairs will cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working while the loader is safe for me and keep our yearly budget review. In 2037 I'd compare the mine's remaining paid shifts with our bills and decide whether to reduce hours; if robots take the loader in 2039, I'd retire only after we have checked our income and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly calm in this picture. Ten years gives us room to decide, and I may be more concerned about my eyesight for night shifts than the robot timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new car now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The current car runs, so we'd wait until it needs replacing rather than buy because of a prediction. Our grown children are independent, and we aren't saving for school fees anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop night shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my eyesight checks show I shouldn't do them safely, I'd ask for day shifts first. I would rather make that choice on a doctor's advice than guess about 2039.

say: I would ask the mine to explain its **long-term plan**.
I would put loader robots around **2039**, after the thinking change.
think: I may already have retired by **71**, but no date is fixed.
Our **future bills** matter more than the savings balance alone.
do: Continue safe **loader work** and review the budget yearly.
Compare **paid shifts** with bills in 2037 before reducing hours.
feel: I feel **fairly calm**, with night-shift eyesight a nearer concern.
S4.quote: I would rather make that choice on a doctor's advice than guess about 2039.
fieldNote: He sees the 2039 robot date through a possible **retirement window**, not a guaranteed exit.
His **eyesight** and current car condition shape immediate choices more than a distant technology forecast.

steps.text: Keep operating the loader while eyesight checks permit safe shifts
Compare 2037 paid shifts with household bills before reducing hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Jo's counter work and my overtime could both change before I have the longer runway to adjust. We would need honest schedules from both employers and paid practice on new equipment if the mine expects me to use it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask enough about the partner's job. A mine worker's savings can look comfortable on paper, but two pay slips decide what the household can actually do.

headlineQuote: A mine worker's savings can look comfortable on paper, but two pay slips decide what the household can actually do.
portrait: Diego is a **58-year-old junior loader operator** at a large mine with better pay than his old delivery job.
He and partner Jo have **grown children** and substantial savings, but have set no retirement date.
He uses AI occasionally and adopts **proven tools** after checking them with experienced operators.
He fears a fast squeeze on **two wages** and looks for paid work and training before leaving the loader.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because Jo’s counter hours and his overtime could shrink together.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **honest schedules** from both employers and paid practice on any new mine controls.
